habitat: Pairs in woodland and around settlements in summer. Small flocks often use vleis in winter. Mostly the drier regions.
summary: An uncommon to fairly common resident and winter visitor. Entirely blue above, including the head and rump, entirely white below, and no tail-shafts. The call is a nasal twitter, chip-cheree-chip-chip. It is sparse, and in many regions, especially the south, it is present only in summer. Newman also calls it a resident and a winter visitor, so status and months were left unset. The Kemp code VB was left unchanged.

similar.note: Wire-tailed Swallow has a full orange cap and wire-like tail-shafts. Pearl-breasted Swallow is blue on the head and rump and has no tail-shafts.

sources.title: The Atlas of Southern African Birds, Vol. 2 (Pearlbreasted Swallow)

population.notes: Kemp et al. 2001 order-of-magnitude threshold 2^8=256 mature individuals (visiting breeder); paper interval half–double → 128–512.

sources.title: Kemp A.C., Herholdt J.J., Whyte I. & Harrison J. (2001). Birds of the two largest national parks in South Africa: a method to generate estimates of population size for all species and assess their conservation ecology. S. Afr. J. Sci. 97: 393–403.

upperparts.pattern: Entirely blue upper parts, including the head and rump. Metallic blue.

viewNotes.note: Blue above, including the head and rump, and white below, with no tail-shafts.
No long tail-shafts. A separate wing pattern was not described.

calls.description: A nasal twitter, chip-cheree-chip-chip. No grade A recording was in the set. Grade B call from the Kap River Nature Reserve. The filename names Pearl-breasted Swallow.

images.author: Liam Huber
images.caption: Pearl-breasted Swallow in the Mopani district. The bird is distant, dark above and pale below, with a forked tail.

research.note: Newman calls it a resident and a winter visitor, and also says it is present only in summer in many regions, especially the south. Status and months were left unset. The Kemp code VB was left unchanged. Population figures were left unchanged. SABAP1 says it occurs all year in the Transvaal but is commoner in winter, from a presumed influx, so status stays omitted.
